items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the balance between the energy received by a surface and the energy lost from it over a period”.
items.answer: Energy budget
items.markingKey: Energy budget: the balance between the energy received by a surface and the energy lost from it over a period. [1]

items.stem: Explain why night-time temperatures fall more on clear nights than on cloudy nights.
items.answer: Without cloud, long-wave radiation escapes to space; clouds absorb outgoing long-wave radiation and re-emit it back (counter-radiation), so heat loss is reduced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark clear sky loss; 1 mark cloud counter-radiation [2]

items.stem: Explain the components of the daytime energy budget.
items.answer: Incoming solar radiation is partly reflected (albedo); some energy is absorbed into the ground (surface absorption); some heats the air by sensible heat transfer; some is used for evaporation (latent heat); the surface emits long-wave radiation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per component [5]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows a midday energy budget (W/m²) for a surface of deciduous forest on a clear day: incoming solar radiation 730; reflected solar radiation 124; net long-wave radiation loss 70; latent heat transfer (evaporation) 267; surface absorption 70; sensible heat transfer to the air: not shown. Suggest why the albedo of this surface could change during the year.
items.answer: Snow cover, leaf fall, crop growth or harvest, wetness, sun angle (especially for water).
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows a midday energy budget (W/m²) for a surface of bare dark soil on a clear day: incoming solar radiation 540; reflected solar radiation 54; net long-wave radiation loss 50; latent heat transfer (evaporation) 183; surface absorption 62; sensible heat transfer to the air: not shown. (a) Calculate the albedo of the surface as a percentage. (b) Suggest why the albedo of this surface could change during the year.
items.answer: (a) 10% (b) Snow cover, leaf fall, crop growth or harvest, wetness, sun angle (especially for water).
items.markingKey: (a) 54 ÷ 540 × 100 [1] (b) 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows a midday energy budget (W/m²) for a surface of desert sand on a clear day: incoming solar radiation 550; reflected solar radiation 220; net long-wave radiation loss 75; latent heat transfer (evaporation) 110; surface absorption 46; sensible heat transfer to the air: not shown. (a) Explain how the budget would differ if the surface were wet. (b) Suggest why the albedo of this surface could change during the year.
items.answer: (a) More energy would be used in evaporation (latent heat), so less would be available for sensible heat transfer and surface temperature would be lower. (b) Snow cover, leaf fall, crop growth or harvest, wetness, sun angle (especially for water).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark latent heat up; 1 mark sensible heat/temperature down [2] (b) 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: “Cloud cover is the most important factor influencing local energy budgets.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to urban surfaces and albedo.
items.answer: For: Clouds reflect incoming solar radiation by day and give counter-radiation at night, so they reduce the diurnal range (e.g. humid tropics v deserts). Against: Surface albedo, moisture availability (latent heat), wind speed (sensible heat), season and latitude (sun angle), and urban surfaces also control budgets. Conclusion: Cloud cover is crucial for the diurnal range, but surface characteristics and sun angle decide how much energy is available in the first place.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “energy budget”?
options: Short-wave radiation from the sun reaching the Earth’s surface.
The proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface.
The balance between the energy received by a surface and the energy lost from it over a period.
Infrared radiation emitted by the Earth’s surface and atmosphere.
items.answer: The balance between the energy received by a surface and the energy lost from it over a period.
items.markingKey: Energy budget: the balance between the energy received by a surface and the energy lost from it over a period. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Surfaces with a high albedo warm up quickly in the sun.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. High albedo surfaces reflect much of the insolation, so less is absorbed and they warm slowly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why a wet soil heats up more slowly than a dry soil during the day.
items.answer: Energy is used in evaporation (latent heat transfer) rather than raising temperature; water has a high specific heat capacity and conducts heat into the soil.
items.markingKey: 1 mark latent heat; 1 mark heat capacity/conduction [2]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows a midday energy budget (W/m²) for a surface of grassland on a clear day: incoming solar radiation 620; reflected solar radiation 155; net long-wave radiation loss 80; latent heat transfer (evaporation) 246; surface absorption 63; sensible heat transfer to the air: not shown. What is the albedo of the surface?

Incoming solar radiation at midday is 520 W/m². Albedo values for four surfaces are: deciduous forest 0.17, bare dark soil 0.1, concrete 0.3, tropical rainforest 0.13. How much solar radiation is absorbed by the concrete?
items.answer: 364 W/m²

items.stem: Incoming solar radiation at midday is 580 W/m². Albedo values for four surfaces are: desert sand 0.4, deciduous forest 0.17, tropical rainforest 0.13, grassland 0.25. (a) Calculate the solar radiation absorbed by the tropical rainforest. (b) Identify which surface would warm most rapidly and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 505 W/m² (b) tropical rainforest: the lowest albedo means the most radiation is absorbed (assuming similar moisture and heat capacity).
items.markingKey: (a) 580 × (1 − 0.13) [2] (b) 1 mark surface; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a layer of the atmosphere in which temperature increases with height”.
items.answer: Temperature inversion
items.markingKey: Temperature inversion: a layer of the atmosphere in which temperature increases with height. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a temperature inversion can form in a valley at night.
items.answer: On clear, calm nights the ground loses heat by radiation and cools the air in contact with it; dense cold air drains downslope into the valley floor, so the coldest air lies beneath warmer air above.
items.markingKey: 1 mark radiation loss; 1 mark cold air drainage; 1 mark warm air above [3]

items.stem: Explain why temperature inversions can lead to severe air pollution in cities.
items.answer: Warm air above cold air is stable, so there is no convection; pollutants are trapped near the ground; e.g. Mexico City, Santiago, Delhi in winter, Los Angeles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stability; 1 mark trapped pollutants; 1 mark example [3]

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 shows air temperatures measured by a weather balloon at dawn in a valley in the Rocky Mountains, USA: 0 m: 1 °C, 100 m: 2.5 °C, 200 m: 4 °C, 300 m: 5.5 °C, 400 m: 7 °C, 500 m: 6.3 °C, 600 m: 5.7 °C. Explain why air pollution is likely to be high in the valley in the morning.
items.answer: The inversion is stable and acts as a lid: there is no convection, so smoke and vehicle emissions are trapped near the ground until the sun heats the surface.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stability; 1 mark trapping [2]

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 shows air temperatures measured by a weather balloon at dawn in a valley near Santiago, Chile: 0 m: -1 °C, 100 m: 0 °C, 200 m: 1 °C, 300 m: 2 °C, 400 m: 3 °C, 500 m: 2.4 °C, 600 m: 1.7 °C. (a) Identify the height of the top of the inversion layer. (b) Explain why air pollution is likely to be high in the valley in the morning.
items.answer: (a) 400 m (b) The inversion is stable and acts as a lid: there is no convection, so smoke and vehicle emissions are trapped near the ground until the sun heats the surface.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark stability; 1 mark trapping [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that temperature inversions are more of a problem in urban areas than in rural areas.
items.answer: For: Inversions trap pollutants from traffic and industry, causing smog (London 1952; Delhi; Mexico City); fog disrupts airports and roads. Against: Rural valleys suffer frost hollows damaging crops and orchards; fog affects rural roads; urban heat islands can weaken inversions in city centres. Conclusion: Urban inversions have the greatest human health impact because of pollution, though rural inversions bring frost and fog hazards.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “fog formed on clear, calm nights when the ground loses heat by radiation and cools the air above it to its dew point”.
items.answer: Radiation fog
items.markingKey: Radiation fog: fog formed on clear, calm nights when the ground loses heat by radiation and cools the air above it to its dew point. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Temperature always falls with height in the lower atmosphere.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. In an inversion temperature rises with height, for example in valleys on clear nights.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between radiation fog and advection fog.
items.answer: Radiation fog forms over land on clear, calm nights by radiative cooling; advection fog forms when moist air moves horizontally over a cold surface such as cold sea or snow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: At 18:00 on a clear, calm autumn evening the air temperature at a weather station was 10 °C and the dew point was 7 °C. The temperature then fell steadily by 1.5 °C per hour. Calculate the time at which the air would reach its dew point.

Fig. 4.2 shows air temperatures measured by a weather balloon at dawn in a valley near Santiago, Chile: 0 m: 0 °C, 100 m: 2.7 °C, 200 m: 5.3 °C, 300 m: 8 °C, 400 m: 7.3 °C, 500 m: 6.7 °C, 600 m: 6 °C. (a) Identify the height of the top of the inversion layer. (b) Explain how the inversion formed.
items.answer: (a) 300 m (b) Clear skies allowed rapid long-wave radiation loss at night; calm conditions; cold dense air drained down the valley sides and settled on the valley floor beneath warmer air.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 shows air temperatures measured by a weather balloon at dawn in a valley near Santiago, Chile: 0 m: 6 °C, 100 m: 7.7 °C, 200 m: 9.3 °C, 300 m: 11 °C, 400 m: 10.3 °C, 500 m: 9.7 °C, 600 m: 9.1 °C. (a) Calculate the rate of temperature change within the inversion layer in °C per 100 m. (b) Explain why air pollution is likely to be high in the valley in the morning.

items.markingKey: (a) 5 °C rise over 300 m [2] (b) 1 mark stability; 1 mark trapping [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the higher temperature of a city compared with the surrounding rural area, greatest on calm, clear nights”.
items.answer: Urban heat island
items.markingKey: Urban heat island: the higher temperature of a city compared with the surrounding rural area, greatest on calm, clear nights. [1]

items.stem: Explain the causes of the urban heat island.
items.answer: Dark surfaces with low albedo absorb insolation; concrete and brick store heat and release it at night; heat from vehicles, industry and air conditioning; less evapotranspiration; pollution dome traps long-wave radiation; urban canyons reduce wind and trap radiation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per cause [5]

items.stem: Explain why urban areas can have more thunderstorms and rainfall than surrounding areas.
items.answer: Higher temperatures cause convection; buildings increase turbulence and uplift; pollution provides condensation nuclei.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Briefly explain why air quality is poor, for Delhi, India or another example of urban air quality management.
items.answer: Delhi, India: Among the world’s most polluted cities: winter PM2.5 often over 300 μg/m³; sources include vehicles, construction dust, industry, and crop-stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana; winter inversions and calm weather trap pollutants.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Physical (relief, inversions, climate) and human causes, with figures. [5]

items.stem: Using one named example of urban air quality management, describe the strategies used to improve air quality.
items.answer: Mexico City: Hoy No Circula (no-drive days by number plate) since 1989; unleaded fuel; refinery closure; Metrobús and bicycle hire (Ecobici); air-quality alerts; ozone has fallen substantially since the 1990s though alerts still occur.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Named policies, dates, effects. [5]

items.stem: Referring to Delhi, India or another example of urban air quality management, evaluate the success of attempts to improve urban air quality.
items.answer: Model answer (Delhi, India): Among the world’s most polluted cities: winter PM2.5 often over 300 μg/m³; sources include vehicles, construction dust, industry, and crop-stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana; winter inversions and calm weather trap pollutants. CNG conversion of buses and auto-rickshaws (2002); Delhi Metro; odd-even car rationing trials (2016); Graded Response Action Plan; closing coal power stations in the city; limited success because sources are regional.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the difference between the urban and rural temperature at the same time”.
items.answer: Urban heat island intensity
items.markingKey: Urban heat island intensity: the difference between the urban and rural temperature at the same time. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Urban areas are always warmer than rural areas at all times of day.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The heat island is strongest at night; by day the difference can be small, and parks can create cool islands.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how urban structures affect wind speeds.
items.answer: Tall buildings increase friction, reducing mean speeds; but funnel winds through urban canyons (Venturi effect) and cause eddies and gusts at the base of tower blocks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.answer: Green roofs and walls; more parks and trees; high-albedo roofs and pavements; water features; reduce waste heat from vehicles.

items.stem: Table 4.3 shows air temperatures (°C) on a calm, clear day in Mumbai. 00:00: city centre 13, rural 9. 04:00: city centre 10.7, rural 4. 08:00: city centre 11.3, rural 10. 12:00: city centre 21.6, rural 21. 16:00: city centre 19.6, rural 19. 20:00: city centre 14, rural 11. items.answer: (a) Greatest at night (max 6.7 °C at 04:00), smallest around midday and afternoon. (b) Buildings and roads release heat stored during the day; urban canyons reduce long-wave radiation loss to the sky (low sky view factor); rural areas cool rapidly by radiation under clear skies.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pattern; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that human activity is the main cause of the distinctive climate of urban areas. In your answer you may refer to heat island, pollution and weather conditions.
items.answer: For: Waste heat, pollution, low-albedo building materials, removal of vegetation and building geometry create the heat island, lower humidity and altered winds. Against: Physical factors (site in a basin or valley, latitude, coastal location, weather type such as calm anticyclones) determine how strongly urban effects show. Conclusion: Urban climates are created by human structures and activity, but weather and site determine their intensity.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “urban heat island”?
options: A street between tall buildings that traps radiation and channels winds.
The difference between the urban and rural temperature at the same time.
A haze formed when sunlight reacts with nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons from vehicles, producing ozone.
The higher temperature of a city compared with the surrounding rural area, greatest on calm, clear nights.
items.answer: The higher temperature of a city compared with the surrounding rural area, greatest on calm, clear nights.
items.markingKey: Urban heat island: the higher temperature of a city compared with the surrounding rural area, greatest on calm, clear nights. [1]

items.stem: Explain how cities can reduce the urban heat island.
items.answer: Green roofs and parks increase evapotranspiration; high-albedo (cool) roofs and pavements; water features; shading trees; reducing waste heat from vehicles and air conditioning.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per strategy explained [4]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the causes of the urban heat island. (b) A revision website states: “Photochemical smog needs strong sunlight to form.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Dark surfaces with low albedo absorb insolation; concrete and brick store heat and release it at night; heat from vehicles, industry and air conditioning; less evapotranspiration; pollution dome traps long-wave radiation; urban canyons reduce wind and trap radiation. (b) Correct. Ultraviolet light drives the reactions between nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons that form ozone.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per cause [5] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Briefly describe the strategies used to improve air quality, for Delhi, India or another example of urban air quality management.
items.answer: Delhi, India: CNG conversion of buses and auto-rickshaws (2002); Delhi Metro; odd-even car rationing trials (2016); Graded Response Action Plan; closing coal power stations in the city; limited success because sources are regional.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Named policies, dates, effects. [5]

(a) Describe the daily pattern of urban heat island intensity. (b) Explain how the heat island would differ on a windy, cloudy day.
items.answer: (a) Greatest at night (max 5 °C at 04:00), smallest around midday and afternoon. (b) Weaker: wind mixes urban and rural air; cloud reduces solar heating by day and radiation loss at night in both areas.

items.stem: For Delhi, India, or another example of urban air quality management you have studied, explain why air quality is poor.
items.answer: Model answer (Delhi, India): Among the world’s most polluted cities: winter PM2.5 often over 300 μg/m³; sources include vehicles, construction dust, industry, and crop-stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana; winter inversions and calm weather trap pollutants.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “short-wave radiation from the sun reaching the Earth’s surface”.
items.answer: Incoming solar radiation (insolation)
items.markingKey: Incoming solar radiation (insolation): short-wave radiation from the sun reaching the Earth’s surface. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Latent heat transfer always causes the surface to lose energy.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Evaporation removes energy, but condensation (dew) releases latent heat to the surface.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why night-time temperatures fall more on clear nights than on cloudy nights. (b) A student writes: “Surfaces with a high albedo warm up quickly in the sun.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Without cloud, long-wave radiation escapes to space; clouds absorb outgoing long-wave radiation and re-emit it back (counter-radiation), so heat loss is reduced. (b) Not correct. High albedo surfaces reflect much of the insolation, so less is absorbed and they warm slowly.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark clear sky loss; 1 mark cloud counter-radiation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Incoming solar radiation at midday is 530 W/m². Albedo values for four surfaces are: fresh snow 0.85, sea ice 0.6, desert sand 0.4, concrete 0.3. How much solar radiation is absorbed by the fresh snow?
items.answer: 80 W/m²

items.answer: 604 W/m²

items.answer: (a) 345 W/m² (b) Snow cover, leaf fall, crop growth or harvest, wetness, sun angle (especially for water).

items.stem: “Cloud cover is the most important factor influencing local energy budgets.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to moisture and albedo.
items.answer: For: Clouds reflect incoming solar radiation by day and give counter-radiation at night, so they reduce the diurnal range (e.g. humid tropics v deserts). Against: Surface albedo, moisture availability (latent heat), wind speed (sensible heat), season and latitude (sun angle), and urban surfaces also control budgets. Conclusion: Cloud cover is crucial for the diurnal range, but surface characteristics and sun angle decide how much energy is available in the first place.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins”.
items.answer: Dew point
items.markingKey: Dew point: the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Fog and cloud are formed by the same process of condensation.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Both form when air cools to its dew point and water vapour condenses on nuclei; fog is simply cloud at ground level.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why radiation fog is more common in autumn and winter. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Wind can prevent radiation fog from forming.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Longer nights allow more cooling; air is often moist; low sun may not clear the fog during the day. (b) Correct. Wind mixes the cold surface air with warmer air above, preventing cooling to dew point.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: At 18:00 on a clear, calm autumn evening the air temperature at a weather station was 9 °C and the dew point was 1 °C. The temperature then fell steadily by 1 °C per hour. Explain how the fog would be affected if the wind speed increased.
items.answer: Turbulent mixing brings warmer, drier air down, raising temperature above dew point and dispersing the fog (or lifting it into low stratus).

items.stem: What is meant by the term “urban heat island intensity”?
options: The difference between the urban and rural temperature at the same time.
A haze formed when sunlight reacts with nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons from vehicles, producing ozone.
Tiny solid or liquid particles less than 2.5 micrometres across, which damage lungs.
A street between tall buildings that traps radiation and channels winds.
items.answer: The difference between the urban and rural temperature at the same time.
items.markingKey: Urban heat island intensity: the difference between the urban and rural temperature at the same time. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Urban areas are always warmer than rural areas at all times of day.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Air pollution in cities can reduce sunshine hours.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. The heat island is strongest at night; by day the difference can be small, and parks can create cool islands. (b) Correct. Particulates scatter and absorb sunlight, reducing direct insolation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why urban areas can have more thunderstorms and rainfall than surrounding areas. (b) Explain how urban structures affect wind speeds.
items.answer: (a) Higher temperatures cause convection; buildings increase turbulence and uplift; pollution provides condensation nuclei. (b) Tall buildings increase friction, reducing mean speeds; but funnel winds through urban canyons (Venturi effect) and cause eddies and gusts at the base of tower blocks.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) 1 mark each [3]
